title: Why we say hello on the phone
hook: Alexander Graham Bell wanted us to answer the telephone with ahoy.
peek: When the telephone was new, nobody knew what to say when it rang. Alexander Graham Bell favoured the sailor's ahoy. Thomas Edison pushed hello, a fairly rare word at the time, and Edison won.
lede: In the 1870s the telephone arrived without any manners. There was no agreed way to open a call, and early users tried all sorts of things. Alexander Graham Bell, its inventor, liked ahoy, borrowed from ships. Thomas Edison, working on rival telephone designs, suggested hello instead. Within a few years hello had won, and it soon spread far beyond the phone.

bullets.text: In a letter of 1877 to a telegraph company executive, Edison argued that a call bell was unnecessary because a shouted hello could be heard 10 to 20 feet away. It is the earliest known record of hello proposed for the phone.
Bell is said to have kept answering with ahoy for the rest of his life, though the evidence is mostly anecdote. The idea lives on as a joke: Mr Burns in The Simpsons answers with ahoy-hoy.
Hello existed before, alongside hallo and hullo, mainly as a shout to get someone's attention or show surprise. It was not yet a polite everyday greeting. The telephone turned it into one.
Early telephone exchanges hired young women to connect calls. By 1889 they were nicknamed hello girls, a sign of how firmly the word had become tied to the phone.
